title: The concept lint rejected
spec: M06 · one required field, and the gate that enforces it
intro: Author an OKF concept from scratch, watch a thirty-line validator throw it out, and fix it. The spec asks for exactly one field — and it is the one everybody forgets, because the five optional ones look more important.

provenance.source: a replayed authoring session in labs/M06-okf-authoring/. Every terminal line matches the output format of labs/M06-okf-authoring/solution/validate.py; the final pass in step 6 carries its own citation.

foot: Do it for real in labs/M06-okf-authoring/ — two concepts and the validator, 25–35 minutes.

steps.title: Choose the path — you have just named the concept
narrative: Before a single character of the file exists, you make the decision that matters most: where it goes. In OKF the file's path is its identity. analytics/metrics/weekly_active_users.md is the concept's ID. There is no UUID, no catalog registry, no page number to keep in sync.

That sounds like a small choice and it kills an entire class of maintenance bug. Every system that mints synthetic IDs eventually drifts from reality — the page moved, the record was cloned, the pointer dangles. When the path is the ID, moving a file is renaming a concept: visible in Git, reviewable in a PR, greppable everywhere it is referenced.
You are documenting orderflow's Weekly Active Users metric — the definition whose absence caused M02's churn-rate disaster. Put it where a person would look for it.

after.title: AND THE FIELD THAT LOOKS REQUIRED BUT IS NOT

view.text: Google's own reference concept carries an id: field in its frontmatter. It is redundant with the path by design — a convenience mirror some producers write, not the identity. If you add one and then move the file, you now have two sources of truth for one fact, which is precisely the drift OKF's path rule was invented to avoid. Write it only if a downstream consumer demands it.

steps.title: Write the frontmatter you think you need
narrative: Here is the draft almost everybody writes first. It is careful work: a real title, an honest description, the owning team, the date it was last touched. It reads like good documentation because it is good documentation.

It is also invalid, and you will not spot why by looking at it — which is the whole point of the next step. Note what the author reached for instinctively: the human-legible fields. The one field the spec actually demands is the least interesting one on the page.
steps.youDo: Fill the stubbed frontmatter in the starter file, then write the body: the rolling 7-day window, completed orders only, and the tester exclusions from services/orders/metrics.py.

before.title: AS AUTHORED — reads fine, fails the spec

lines: description: Unique customers with at least one completed order in a rolling 7-day window, excluding internal test accounts.
The total unique count of `customer_id` values with at least one completed
order whose `completed_at` falls inside a rolling 7-day window.

steps.title: Lint throws it out
narrative: Thirty lines of Python, one hard rule. It walks every .md under knowledge/, skips the two reserved filenames, and refuses anything without a type.

Read the summary line carefully: zero concepts valid. Not "one concept with a warning" — the file does not count as a concept at all, because type is what tells a consumer what kind of thing it is holding. Everything else in that frontmatter is colour.
The exit code is the part that matters operationally. A lint that prints a red line and returns 0 is decoration; this one stops a pipeline.
steps.youDo: python validate.py knowledge, then echo $? to confirm you actually got a non-zero exit and not just a scary-looking log line.

terminal.text: exit 1 — nothing downstream runs. No agent is allowed to read this bundle.

state.label: what the spec asks for vs what you wrote

steps.title: One line fixes it — and reveals what the spec never asked for
narrative: Add type: metric. That is the fix. The validator now counts a concept, and immediately starts telling you about things the spec does not care about at all.

Those warn lines are your lint being stricter than the format. OKF would happily accept a file whose entire frontmatter is type: metric — no title, no description, nothing. Your pipeline refuses to be that relaxed, and it says so without failing the build.
Learn to read the two levels apart. Errors are the spec's floor. Warnings are your team's standard. Confusing them is how teams end up either shipping garbage or arguing about a linter.
steps.youDo: Add the required field, then close the three warnings by adding resource: ../../sample-project/services/orders/metrics.py, tags: [analytics, orders, canonical] and a timestamp.

before.title: THE FIX — one required line, three recommended ones

lines: description: Unique customers with at least one completed order in a rolling 7-day window, excluding internal test accounts.

after.title: WHY THE LAST TWO LINES CAME OUT

view.text: owner and updated_at were legal — consumers must tolerate unknown keys — but timestamp now says the same thing as updated_at, and two fields carrying one fact is the drift you are here to prevent. Keep unknown keys when they add information your team needs; delete them when they duplicate a recommended field.

steps.title: The link is an edge — and nothing will ever check it for you
narrative: A metric is not knowledge on its own. WAU reads the orders_fact table, and that relationship is what turns a folder of Markdown into a graph. You write it as an ordinary relative link and the folder becomes traversable.

OKF links are untyped: the link is just a link, and the relationship's meaning lives in the prose around it — "reads", "joined with", "see also". That is a deliberate ceiling. Track 2's AST edges are typed and verified; these are curated. You want both.

Now the trap. The spec says a conformant consumer must not reject a bundle for broken links. So write a link to a file that does not exist yet, and the format is perfectly happy. Only a check you wrote yourself will ever say a word.
steps.youDo: Add - See [orders_fact](../tables/orders_fact.md) for the fact table this metric reads. under a ## Related Components heading — before you have written orders_fact.md.

terminal.text: clean — and the only link in the bundle points at a file that does not exist

before.title: WHAT THE SPEC TOLERATES BY DESIGN

cells: yes — there is no type registry
a link to a file that does not exist

view.text: The spec is lenient so that adoption is easy — a team can start with one file today and be conformant, which is why OKF spread in weeks while schema-registry predecessors stalled for years. Your pipeline must be strict so that trust is possible. A bundle of dangling links, drifted type names and year-old timestamps is still technically conformant, and nothing anywhere will error. That gap is M11's entire subject.

steps.title: What a valid concept looks like when it passes
narrative: Write the other side of the link — orders_fact.md, with its schema table, a Joins section and a link back to the metric — and run the gate on the whole bundle.

Two concepts, zero errors, both directions of the edge present. Read the finished WAU file once more as an agent would: forty tokens of frontmatter answer is this relevant?, the body carries the audited exclusion rule itself rather than a pointer to where the rule lives, and the link hands over the next hop. An agent computing WAU generates the right query on the first attempt and can cite the file, its timestamp and its owner.
That is the whole consumption stack. No SDK, no schema registry, no service — cat to read it, git clone to ship it, thirty lines to gate it.
steps.youDo: python validate.py knowledge — you should see the exact line in expected_output/sample_output.txt. Then break it on purpose: delete type: from one file and confirm you get a non-zero exit and the offending path.
